stem: A tangent curve has an equation of the form $y=a\tan\theta+q$. Point $A$ is at $\left(0^{\circ}, {=q}\right)$ and point $B$ is at $\left(45^{\circ}, {=yb}\right)$; both points lie on the curve. Determine the values of $a$ and $q$.
solution: The constant $q$ shifts the graph up or down. For an unshifted tangent graph, point $A$ would be at $\left(0^{\circ}, 0\right)$. Here $A$ is at $\left(0^{\circ}, {=q}\right)$, so the graph has been shifted upwards by ${=q}$. Therefore $q={=q}$.
To find $a$, substitute $q={=q}$ and point $B$, $\left(45^{\circ}, {=yb}\right)$, into the equation. Remember that $\tan 45^{\circ}=1$.
The complete equation is $y={=a}\tan\theta+{=q}$. Therefore $a={=a}$ and $q={=q}$.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Takes the y-value of B as a
proposed_misconceptions.description: Reads a straight off the y-coordinate of point B (a = y_B) because tan 45 degrees is 1, forgetting that the graph is shifted by q, so a = y_B is given instead of a = y_B - q.

notes: Entry point of the skill: both a and q positive integers, second point at 45 degrees where tan = 1, so y_B = a + q. Models ex6-6-6 and the upward-shift half of ex6-6-5. The book's figure is not reproduced (the family format carries no image): both labelled points are given in words as coordinates, exactly as the book's stems state them. a starts at 2 so the stated equation never reads 1tan. a != q so the two values are never confusable in the answer.
